title: Time and Work
tagline: Year 2 — Rates of work, working together, leaving early and alternate days

introduction.overview: Time and work problems ask how long a job takes when one or more workers do it alone or together. The central idea is the rate of work: a worker who completes a job in n days does 1/n of the job per day. Rates of workers who work together add. Everything else, including leaving early, joining late and alternate days, is bookkeeping on these rates.
introduction.placementRelevance: Time and work questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds and are a regular intermediate-level item, often with two or three workers and one twist.
introduction.realWorldContext: Estimating the time to finish a project with several people, or how long a team needs after some members leave, uses the same idea.

learningObjectives: Convert days into work rates and add them
Solve problems with two or three workers working together
Use man-days for men, hours-per-day problems

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: If a worker does a job in n days, the rate is 1/n job per day. In t days they do t/n of the job.

coreDefinitions: Rate of work: the fraction of the job done per unit time (1/n per day).
Combined rate: the sum of individual rates when workers work together.
Man-days: number of men × number of days; a measure of the total work.
Efficiency: how fast a worker works; ratio of efficiencies is the inverse of the ratio of times.
Alternate-day work: workers take turns, each day a different worker works.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Think of the job as 1. If A needs 10 days and B needs 15 days, A does 1/10 and B 1/15 each day. Together they do 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 per day, so the job takes 6 days. A faster worker has a bigger rate and a shorter time.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: To avoid fractions, pick a convenient total work, the LCM of the days. For 10 and 15 days take 30 units: A does 3 units a day, B 2 units, together 5 units a day, so 30 ÷ 5 = 6 days.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Rate and time
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: n is the time taken alone.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Man-days
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: M₁ D₁ H₁ = M₂ D₂ H₂
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Men × days × hours per day is constant for one job.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Efficiency
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: A is twice as efficient as B.

mainNarrative: Start with rates. A worker who takes 12 days does 1/12 of the work each day, so in 3 days they do 3/12 = 1/4. For two workers the combined rate is the sum, and the time is its reciprocal.

Use the LCM method to avoid fractions: take the total work as the LCM of the times. If A takes 20 days and B 30 days, the total is 60 units. A does 3 units/day and B 2 units/day, together 5 units/day, so 12 days.

For a worker who joins late or leaves early, compute the work done before the change, subtract from 1, and divide the remainder by the new combined rate. A (20 days) works 5 days alone: 1/4 done. Then A and B together (rate 1/12) finish the remaining 3/4 in 9 days, total 14 days.
For men and days, use man-days. 12 men finishing a job in 18 days is 216 man-days. After 6 days, 72 man-days are done and 144 remain. With 8 men that is 18 more days.

For alternate days, find the work done in a pair of days and see how many full pairs fit. If A (12 days) and B (18 days) work alternately, a pair does 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36. After 14 days (7 pairs) 35/36 is done and A completes the last 1/36 on day 15.

deepDiveAspects.title: Rate, not time, adds
deepDiveAspects.content: Times cannot be added for workers working together; rates can. The combined time is always shorter than the faster worker's time.

deepDiveAspects.title: Working against each other
deepDiveAspects.content: Pipes and cisterns are the same idea with a negative rate for a leak or outlet. Time-and-work techniques apply directly.

problemVariations.exampleSnippet: A 10 days, B 15 days, C 30 days
A leaves 5 days before the end
A is twice as good as B

solvedExamples.title: Working together
solvedExamples.question: A can do a piece of work in 10 days and B in 15 days. In how many days can they do it together?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The combined rate is the sum of the rates.

solvedExamples.title: Joining late
solvedExamples.question: A can do a work in 20 days and B in 30 days. A starts and works for 5 days, then B joins. In how many days in all is the work finished?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The total includes the first 5 days.

solvedExamples.title: Men and days
solvedExamples.question: 12 men can complete a work in 18 days. After 6 days, 4 men leave. In how many more days will the remaining men finish the work?
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using 12 men for the remaining days.

shortcutMethods.title: LCM units

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Add fractions of the work each time.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Take the LCM of all days as the total units, find each worker's units per day, add and divide.

rulesForApplication: Faster worker has a bigger rate.
Subtract the work done before changes in the team.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using the efficiency ratio as the time ratio.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring that leaving workers still did their part
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming workers who left did nothing.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The combined time must be less than the shortest individual time.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Use LCM units and a quick table of units per day.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: This is the base for work and wages and for pipes and cisterns.

advanced.question: A and B can finish a job in 30 and 20 days. They start together but A leaves 5 days before the job is finished. The job takes
advanced.explanation: Let the time be t. t/20 + (t − 5)/30 = 1 gives 3t + 2t − 10 = 60, so t = 14.

advanced.question: A and B together can do a work in 6 days. A alone takes 5 days less than B alone. A alone takes
advanced.explanation: Let A = x and B = x + 5. 1/x + 1/(x + 5) = 1/6 gives x² − 7x − 30 = 0, so x = 10.

placementStyle.question: A can do 1/3 of a work in 4 days and B can do 1/4 of it in 6 days. Together they can do the whole work in
placementStyle.explanation: A alone = 12 days and B alone = 24 days. 1/12 + 1/24 = 1/8, so 8 days.

placementStyle.explanation: Total = 300 man-days. 150 done in 10 days. 10 men do the remaining 150 in 15 days. Total 25 days.
